# Information theory (bit, entropy, channel capacity) (`information_theory`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs probability_statistics, logarithms; helped by binary_numbers, electric_telegraph, telephone, cryptography
- Core idea: Information can be measured, whatever its meaning. The unit is the bit, one choice between two equally likely alternatives; picking one of eight equally likely messages is three bits. A source that prefers some messages to others carries less: on average the sum over all messages of p times log2(1/p) bits, its entropy, and lossless coding of long independent blocks can approach that average per message (English text needs only about one bit per letter, against nearly five if all letters were equally likely). Every channel has a capacity in bits per second, for an ideal band-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise, bandwidth B and average signal-to-noise power ratio S/N, the capacity is B times log2(1 + S/N). Below that rate, messages can be sent with as few errors as one likes, by coding in long blocks with well chosen redundancy; above it they cannot. Noise limits the rate of a channel, not its accuracy.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing information with meaning or value; the measure concerns only how many alternatives a message rules out
  - Believing that noise can only be fought with more power or by repeating the message; coding does far better
  - Reading the theorem as a recipe; Shannon proved that good codes exist, finding practical ones took fifty years
  - Using 'entropy' loosely for disorder, or applying the formulas to psychology and art, which Shannon himself warned against in 1956
- History: europe: 1915, 1933 – sampling theorem (Whittaker in Edinburgh, Kotelnikov in Moscow); 1946 Gabor's theory of communication (London); americas: 1924–1928 – Nyquist and Hartley at Bell Labs relate telegraph speed and bandwidth and propose a logarithmic measure; 1948 Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (Bell Labs), where Shannon credits the contraction ‘bit’ to Tukey; 1948 Wiener's Cybernetics treats the same measure independently; 1952 Huffman's optimal codes
- Read:
  - Claude E. Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, Bell System Technical Journal 27 (1948)
  - John R. Pierce, Symbols, Signals and Noise: The Nature and Process of Communication (1961)
  - James Gleick, The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood (2011)
